title: Exam 4 Numbers to Know
description: Exam 4 drill, matched to the instructor's study guide: the numbers to know, from the diabetes, cholesterol, and metabolic syndrome cutoffs to the blood gas ranges, capillary refill, the QRS, the lungs' lobes and segments, and more. Most questions show a new number on every attempt.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher is in the diabetes range; {g} mg/dL is over that line.

Prediabetes is the tempting choice when the number is close to the line, but prediabetes stops at 125.

Takeaway: Fasting glucose: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes; under 70 is low.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is prediabetes; {g} mg/dL falls in it.

Normal is the tempting choice, since the number is close to 100, but normal is under 100.

Takeaway: Fasting glucose: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes; under 70 is low.

questions.stem: A client's fasting plasma glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL (and at least 70) is normal; {g} mg/dL is in that range.

Prediabetes is the tempting choice when the number is in the high 90s, but prediabetes starts at 100.

Takeaway: Fasting glucose: under 100 normal, 100 to 125 prediabetes, 126 or higher diabetes; under 70 is low.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is {a}%. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
An A1C of 6.5% or higher is in the diabetes range; {a}% is at or over that line.

Prediabetes is the tempting choice for a number just over 6.4, but 6.5% is already diabetes.

Takeaway: A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is {a}%. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
An A1C of 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes, and the instructor's guide lists an A1C over 5.7% as a risk factor for diabetes; {a}% is in that range.

Normal is the tempting choice, since the number is under 6.5, but normal is under 5.7%.

Takeaway: A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is {a}%. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
An A1C under 5.7% is normal; {a}% is in that range.

Prediabetes is the tempting choice when the number is in the mid-5s, but prediabetes starts at 5.7%.

Takeaway: A1C: under 5.7% normal, 5.7% to 6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: Two hours after a 75-g glucose drink, a client's glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
Two hours after the glucose drink, 200 mg/dL or higher is in the diabetes range; {g} mg/dL is at or over it.

Prediabetes is the tempting choice, since the fasting cutoffs are lower, but the 2-hour test has its own: 140 to 199 is prediabetes.

Takeaway: 2-hour glucose: under 140 normal, 140 to 199 prediabetes, 200 or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: Two hours after a 75-g glucose drink, a client's glucose is {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
Two hours after the glucose drink, 140 to 199 mg/dL is prediabetes; {g} mg/dL falls in it.

The diabetes range is the tempting choice, since {g} is well over the fasting cutoff of 126, but the 2-hour test's diabetes line is 200.

Takeaway: 2-hour glucose: under 140 normal, 140 to 199 prediabetes, 200 or higher diabetes.

questions.stem: A client who is sweaty and shaky has a fingerstick glucose of {g} mg/dL. Which range is this result in?
questions.rationale:
A glucose under 70 mg/dL is low (hypoglycemia), and sweating and shakiness are its classic signs; {g} mg/dL is in that range.

The normal range is the tempting choice for a number in the 60s, but normal starts at 70.

Takeaway: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia: treat it quickly.

questions.stem: A client with constant thirst and frequent urination has a random glucose of {g} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: It needs a fasting test before it can mean anything
It's normal for a sample taken at a random time
It's in the prediabetes range, since it wasn't fasting
It's in the diabetes range, since the client has symptoms
questions.rationale:
A random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms (thirst, frequent urination, weight loss) meets the criteria for diabetes; {g} mg/dL with these symptoms does.

Needing a fasting test is the tempting choice, since one random result usually isn't enough, but symptoms plus a random glucose of 200 or more is one of the four criteria.

Takeaway: Random glucose 200 or higher with symptoms = diabetes range.

questions.stem: A client's total cholesterol is {tc} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
A risk factor for heart disease
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide lists a total cholesterol over 200 mg/dL as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease; {tc} mg/dL is over it.

Borderline is the tempting choice for a number just over 200, but the guide's line is 200: anything over it counts.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's total cholesterol is {tc} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
A total cholesterol under 200 mg/dL isn't a risk factor by the instructor's cutoff; {tc} mg/dL is under it.

A risk factor is the tempting choice when the number is in the 190s, but the line is 200.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's LDL is {ldl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
An LDL over 100 mg/dL is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease; {ldl} mg/dL is over it.

Within the desired range is the tempting choice if you use the total cholesterol line (200), but LDL has its own: 100.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's LDL is {ldl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
An LDL under 100 mg/dL isn't a risk factor by the instructor's cutoff; {ldl} mg/dL is under it.

Too low is the tempting choice for a low number, but a low LDL is the goal, not a problem.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A woman's HDL is {hdl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
For women, an HDL under 50 mg/dL is a risk factor; {hdl} mg/dL is under it.

Within the desired range is the tempting choice if you use the men's line (40), but for women it's 50.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A man's HDL is {hdl} mg/dL. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: A risk factor for heart disease
Borderline, but not yet a risk factor
Too low, a sign of poor nutrition
questions.rationale:
For men, an HDL under 40 mg/dL is a risk factor; {hdl} mg/dL is above it, so it isn't one.

A risk factor is the tempting choice if you use the women's line (50), but for men it's 40.

Takeaway: Risk factors: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women).

questions.stem: A client's body mass index (BMI) is {b}. How should the nurse interpret it?
options: A risk factor for diabetes and heart disease
Not a risk factor for either disease
A sign of malnutrition and weight loss
A risk factor for diabetes but not heart disease
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide lists a BMI over 25 as a risk factor for both diabetes and cardiovascular disease; {b} is over it.

A risk factor for diabetes but not heart disease is the tempting choice, since BMI comes up in diabetes screening, but the guide lists it for heart disease too.

Takeaway: BMI over 25: a risk factor for diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

questions.stem: A client's body mass index (BMI) is {b}. How should the nurse interpret it?
options: Not a risk factor for either disease
A risk factor for diabetes and heart disease
A sign of malnutrition and weight loss
A risk factor for diabetes but not heart disease
questions.rationale:
A BMI of 25 or under isn't on the instructor's list of risk factors; {b} is under it.

A risk factor is the tempting choice when the number is close to 25, but the line is over 25.

Takeaway: BMI over 25: a risk factor for diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

questions.stem: A man's waist is {w} in., his triglycerides are {tg} mg/dL, his HDL is {hdl} mg/dL, his blood pressure is {sbp}/{dbp} mm Hg, and his fasting glucose is {fg} mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria does he meet?
options: 1, so he doesn't have metabolic syndrome
2, so he doesn't have metabolic syndrome
questions.rationale:
He meets two: a waist of {w} in. (about 40 or more for men) and triglycerides of {tg} (150 or more). His HDL of {hdl} isn't low for a man (under 40), his blood pressure is under 130/85, and his glucose is under 100. Metabolic syndrome needs 3 or more.

3 is the tempting choice if you count his HDL as low, but for men the line is 40.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 or more of waist, triglycerides, low HDL, blood pressure, fasting glucose.

questions.stem: A woman's waist is {w} in., her triglycerides are {tg} mg/dL, her HDL is {hdl} mg/dL, her blood pressure is {sbp}/{dbp} mm Hg, and her fasting glucose is {fg} mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria does she meet?
options: 2, so she doesn't have metabolic syndrome
1, so she doesn't have metabolic syndrome
questions.rationale:
She meets three: a waist of {w} in. (35 or more for women), an HDL of {hdl} (under 50 for women), and a blood pressure of {sbp}/{dbp} (130/85 or more). Her triglycerides are under 150 and her glucose under 100. Three criteria means metabolic syndrome.

2 is the tempting choice if you use the men's HDL line (40), which would make her HDL normal.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 or more of waist, triglycerides, low HDL, blood pressure, fasting glucose.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a client's capillary refill, and the color returns in {s} seconds. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Normal: blood flow to the tissues is good
Slow, but expected in any older adult
Slow: blood flow to the tissues is reduced
Too fast, a sign of high blood pressure
questions.rationale:
Capillary refill measures peripheral perfusion. Color should return in about 2 seconds (no more than 3); {s} seconds is slow, so blood flow to the tissues is reduced.

Expected in older adults is the tempting choice, but a slow refill needs follow-up at any age.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: about 2 seconds, no more than 3.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a client's capillary refill, and the color returns in {s} seconds. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Slow: blood flow to the tissues is reduced
Slow, but expected in any older adult
Too fast, a sign of high blood pressure
Normal: blood flow to the tissues is good
questions.rationale:
Color returning in about 2 seconds or less shows good blood flow to the tissues; {s} seconds is normal.

Too fast is the tempting choice, since quick sounds abnormal, but a quick refill just means good perfusion.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: about 2 seconds, no more than 3.

questions.stem: A client's QRS complex measures {q} seconds on the ECG. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Normal for a P wave, not a QRS
questions.rationale:
The QRS shows the ventricles depolarizing and is normally under 0.12 seconds (120 ms); {q} seconds is wide, so the ventricles are depolarizing slowly: report it.

Within the normal width is the tempting choice, since the number is small, but the QRS line is 0.12.

Takeaway: QRS under 0.12 seconds is normal; wider needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A client's QRS complex measures {q} seconds on the ECG. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Normal for a P wave, not a QRS
questions.rationale:
A QRS under 0.12 seconds is normal; {q} seconds is within it.

Narrower than normal is the tempting choice for a small number, but a narrow QRS is the normal finding.

Takeaway: QRS under 0.12 seconds is normal; wider needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the blood. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Plasma makes up about {{0}} of the blood, and red blood cells live about {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
Plasma, the liquid part (mostly water, with salts, proteins, hormones, and vitamins), is about 55% of the blood; the formed elements are about 45%. Red cells live about 120 days.

The tempting mistake is 90%: that's about how much of the plasma is water.

Takeaway: Plasma about 55%; red cells live about 120 days.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing normal arterial blood gases. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: A normal pH is {{0}}, a normal PaCO₂ is {{1}}, and a normal HCO₃⁻ is {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Normal: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L.

The tempting mistake is 80 to 100 for the PaCO₂: that's the normal PaO₂ (oxygen).

Takeaway: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing normal arterial blood gases. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: A normal PaO₂ is {{0}}, and a normal base excess is {{1}}.
questions.rationale:
Normal: PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg and base excess −2 to +2 mEq/L. Below −2 means too little base (metabolic acidosis); above +2, too much (metabolic alkalosis).

The tempting mistake is a base excess range of 0 to +4, since “excess” sounds positive; normal is centered on zero.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80–100; base excess −2 to +2.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lungs. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The right lung has {{0}} lobes and {{1}} segments; the left lung has {{2}} lobes and {{3}} segments.
questions.rationale:
Right lung: 3 lobes, 10 segments. Left lung: 2 lobes, 8 to 9 segments, leaving room for the heart.

The tempting mistake is giving the left lung 3 lobes; the lingula is part of the left upper lobe.

Takeaway: Right 3 and 10; left 2 and 8 to 9.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client breathing room air has a PaO₂ of {p} mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this value?
options: It can't be judged without the pH
questions.rationale:
A normal PaO₂ is 80 to 100 mm Hg; {p} is below it, so the blood is carrying too little oxygen.

It can't be judged without the pH is the tempting choice, since blood gases are read together, but each value has its own normal range.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80 to 100 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client breathing room air has a PaO₂ of {p} mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this value?
options: It can't be judged without the pH
questions.rationale:
A normal PaO₂ is 80 to 100 mm Hg; {p} is within it.

Below the normal range is the tempting choice for a number in the 80s, but normal starts at 80.

Takeaway: PaO₂ 80 to 100 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A client's phrenic nerve, which controls the diaphragm, was injured. From which level of the spinal cord does this nerve come?
questions.rationale:
The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5 in the neck, which is why a high neck injury can stop the diaphragm.

T1 to T4 is the tempting choice, since the diaphragm sits in the trunk, but its nerve starts high in the neck.

Takeaway: “C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.”

questions.stem: A client walks {m} minutes on {d} days a week. How many more minutes a week does the client need to reach the goal of 150 minutes?
questions.rationale:
The client walks {m} × {d} = {=m * d} minutes a week. The instructor's goal is 150 minutes a week (for example 20 to 30 minutes on 5 to 7 days), so the client needs 150 − {=m * d} = {answer} more minutes.

The tempting mistake is subtracting the daily minutes ({m}) instead of the weekly total.

Takeaway: Exercise goal: about 150 minutes a week.

questions.stem: A client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (normal about 0.4 to 4.0). Which condition does this result suggest?
options: A problem with the parathyroid glands
questions.rationale:
TSH is the pituitary's signal to the thyroid. A high TSH ({t}) means the pituitary is pushing harder because the thyroid isn't keeping up: an underactive thyroid.

An overactive thyroid is the tempting choice, since a high number sounds like “too much”, but a high TSH usually means too little thyroid hormone.

Takeaway: High TSH: underactive thyroid. Low TSH: overactive thyroid.

questions.stem: A client's TSH is {t} mIU/L (normal about 0.4 to 4.0). Which condition does this result suggest?
options: A problem with the parathyroid glands
questions.rationale:
A low TSH ({t}) means the pituitary has backed off because there's plenty of thyroid hormone: an overactive thyroid.

An underactive thyroid is the tempting choice, since a low number sounds like “too little”, but the thyroid hormone itself is high.

Takeaway: High TSH: underactive thyroid. Low TSH: overactive thyroid.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the stages of inflammation. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Acute inflammation lasts {{0}}, subacute inflammation lasts about {{1}}, and chronic inflammation lasts {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Acute inflammation starts within minutes to hours and lasts days; subacute lasts about 2 to 6 weeks; chronic lasts months or longer.

The tempting mistake is 2 to 6 days for subacute, which is still the acute stage.

Takeaway: Acute: days. Subacute: 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic: months or longer.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing immunity. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The first specific (adaptive) response to a new germ takes about {{0}}, the flu vaccine is given {{1}}, and adults should exercise about {{2}} a week.
questions.rationale:
The adaptive response to a new germ takes about 4 to 7 days to build. The flu vaccine is given every year (the viruses change), and the exercise goal is about 150 minutes a week.

The tempting mistake is 1 to 2 days: that's how fast the innate defenses (like inflammation) respond.

Takeaway: Adaptive response 4 to 7 days; flu vaccine yearly; exercise 150 minutes a week.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing cortisol. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: Cortisol is highest in the {{0}} and lowest around {{1}}, so a blood test is usually drawn at about {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
Cortisol follows a daily rhythm: highest in the early morning, lowest around midnight. A morning blood test (about 8 a.m.) catches the peak.

The tempting mistake is the evening, when people often feel most stressed; cortisol is actually falling then.

Takeaway: Cortisol: high in the morning, low at midnight.
